The Origin of Species

  • In the 150 years since the publication of Darwin’s book On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, new discoveries and technological advances have given scientists a wealth of new information about the evolution of life.
  • The diversity of life evolved through speciation, the process in which one species splits into two or more species.

A Marine Iguana (Right), An Example of the Unique Species Inhabiting the Galápagos

Text description of this image

A photo shows a land-dwelling iguana on a branch with a rounded tail. A photo shows a marine iguana with a flattened tail on a rock.

What is a Species?

  • Species is a Latin word meaning “kind” or “appearance.”
  • The biological species concept defines a species as “a group of populations whose members have the potential to interbreed with one another in nature and produce fertile offspring (offspring that can reproduce).”
  • The biological species concept cannot be applied in all situations, including asexual organisms and fossils.

The Biological Species Concept is Based on Reproductive Compatibility Rather than Physical Similarity

Text description of this image

A composite of two photos shows two yellow songbirds with gray and black markings; one appears slim while the other appears stout. A composite of six photos shows human faces, including three women and men with varying skin tone, hair type, and facial features.

Reproductive Barriers Between Closely Related Species

Text description of this image

Two individuals of different species are prevented from a mating attempt by prezygotic barriers. These include:; Temporal isolation: Mating or fertilization occurs at different seasons or times of day.; Habitat isolation: Populations live in different habitats and do not meet.; Behavioral isolation: Little or no sexual attraction exists between populations.; Two additional prezygotic barriers prevent the formation of a zygote even if mating were attempted. These are:; Mechanical isolation: Structural differences prevent fertilization.; Gametic isolation: Female and male gametes fail to unite in fertilization.; If fertilization occurs and the zygote forms, postzygotic barriers prevent the formation of viable, fertile offspring. These are:; Reduced hybrid viability: Hybrid zygotes fail to develop or fail to reach sexual maturity.; Reduced hybrid fertility: Hybrids fail to produce functional gametes.; Hybrid breakdown: Hybrids are feeble or sterile.; When there are no barriers, viable, fertile offspring can form.

Prezygotic Barriers

Text description of this image

Temporal isolation: The corresponding photos show two black-and-white skunks with one seated on leaves and the other on bare ground. These two closely related species of skunks mate at different times of the year.; Habitat isolation: The corresponding photos show two garter snakes; one swims with its head above water and the other moves through vegetation. These two closely related species of garter snakes do not mate because one lives in the water and the other lives on land and The figure shows the following:; Behavioral isolation: A photo shows two blue-footed boobies (one is larger than the other) making stepping motions with their bright blue webbed feet. Galápagos blue-footed boobies mate only after a specific ritual of high stepping that advertises a mate’s bright blue feet.; Mechanical isolation: A photo shows two snails with their head and abdomen regions intertwined; their genital regions are just behind the heads and do not line up. The shells spiral in opposite directions. The short, straight bill of this hummingbird is compatible with the flower on the left but does not fit the curved flower on the right. Thus, pollen is not transferred between these two plant species.; Gametic isolation: A photo shows a red sea urchin surrounded by purple sea urchins. Gametes of these red and purple urchins are unable to fuse because proteins on the surface of the eggs and sperm cannot bind to one another.

Postzygotic Barriers

Text description of this image

Reduced hybrid viability: A photo shows an orange salamander with dark spots. Some species of salamander can hybridize, but their offspring do not develop fully or, like this one, are frail and will not survive long enough to reproduce.; Reduced hybrid fertility: The figure shows a horse, donkey, and a mule. The hybrid offspring of a horse and a donkey is a mule, which is sterile.; Hybrid breakdown: A photo shows three rice plants: the plants on the left and right are tall and thick and the plant in the middle is small and thin. The rice hybrids at the left and right are fertile, but plants of the next generation (middle) are sterile.

Evolution: Mechanisms of Speciation

  • A key event in the origin of a species occurs when a population is somehow cut off from other populations of the parent species.
  • Species can form by
    • allopatric speciation, in which the initial block to gene flow is a geographic barrier that physically isolates the splinter population,
    • sympatric speciation, without geographic isolation.

Allopatric Speciation of Antelope Squirrels on Opposite Rims of the Grand Canyon

Text description of this image

A photo shows the Grand Canyon with insets of two antelope squirrels, Ammospermophilus harrisii and Ammospermophilus leucurus, on opposite rims of the canyon.

Possible Outcomes After Geographic Isolation of Populations

Text description of this image

Two populations are shown becoming allopatric as a geographic barrier (in this case, a mountain range) divides the populations into separate groups.; The top image shows that as the populations become sympatric again (come back together in the same location on the other side of the mountain range), the populations that were separated can still interbreed. The gene pools merge, so no speciation has occurred.; The bottom image shows that, as the populations become sympatric again, they cannot interbreed. Reproductive isolation has occurred, thus speciation has occurred.

Sympatric Speciation in a Plant

Text description of this image

Species A (2n equals to 4; 4 chromosomes in two homologous pairs are drawn); Species A produces a gamete that is n equals to 2 (two chromosomes); Species B (2n equals to 6; six chromosomes in three pairs are drawn); Species B produces a gamete that is n equals to 3 (three chromosomes).; Following fertilization, a sterile hybrid is produced because the chromosomes from gamete A and gamete B cannot pair.; The sterile hybrid is n equals to 5 and has five chromosomes; two from gamete A and three from gamete B. The sterile hybrid can reproduce asexually.; Following asexual reproduction, a viable, fertile hybrid species is produced that is 2n equals to 10 (has ten chromosomes in five pairs; the ten chromosomes are made up of pairs of the five single chromosomes that were present in the sterile hybrid).

The Fossil Record

  • Fossils are evidence of organisms that lived in the past. The fossil record is the sequence in which fossils appear in rock strata and an archive of macroevolution.
  • The geologic time scale divides Earth’s history into a consistent sequence of geologic periods.

Strata of Sedimentary Rock at the Grand Canyon

The Geologic Time Scale

Text description of this image

A table illustrates the geologic time scale, providing details of the geologic time, period, epoch, age in millions of years ago, and some important events in the history of life. The details of the table are as follows: 1. Geologic time: Cenozoic era i. Period: Quaternary

Epoch: Holocene; Age: 0.01; Event: Historical time; Epoch: Pleistocene; Age: 2.6; Event: Ice ages; humans appear

ii. Period: Tertiary

Epoch: Pliocene; Age: 5.3; Event: Origin of genus Homo; Epoch: Miocene; Age: 23; Event: Continued speciation of mammals and angiosperms; Epoch: Oligocene; Age: 34; Event: Origins of many primate groups, including apes; Epoch: Eocene; Age: 56; Event: Angiosperm dominance increases; origins of most living mammalian orders; Epoch: Paleocene; Age: 66; Event: Major speciation of mammals, birds, and pollinating insects

2. Geologic time: Mesozoic era i. Period: Cretaceous

Age: 145; Event: Flowering plants (angiosperms) appear; many groups of organisms, including most dinosaur lineages, become extinct at end of period (Cretaceous extinctions)

ii. Period: Jurassic

Age: 201; Event: Gymnosperms continue as dominant plants; dinosaurs become dominant

iii. Period: Triassic

Age: 252; Event: Cone-bearing plants (gymnosperms) dominate landscape; speciation of dinosaurs, early mammals, and birds

3. Geologic time: Paleozoic era i. Period: Permian

Age: 299; Event: Extinction of many marine and terrestrial organism (Permian extinctions); speciation of reptiles; origins of mammal-like reptiles and most living orders of insects

ii. Period: Carboniferous

Age: 359; Event: Extensive forests of vascular plants; first seed plants; origin of reptiles; amphibians become dominant

iii. Period: Devonian

Age: 419; Event: Diversification of bony fishes; first amphibians and insects

iv. Period: Silurian

Age: 444; Event: Early vascular plants dominate land

v. Period: Ordovician

Age: 488; Event: Marine algae are abundant; colonization of land by diverse fungi, plants, and animals

vi. Period: Cambrian

Age: 541; Event: Sudden increase in diversity of many animal phyla (Cambrian explosion)

4. Geologic time: Precambrian

Age: 600; Event: Diverse algae and soft-bodied invertebrate animals appear; Age: 635; Event: Oldest animal fossils; Age: 1,200; Event: Oldest known fossils of multicellular organisms; Age: 1,800; Event: Oldest fossils of eukaryotic cells; Age: 2,700; Event: Oxygen begins accumulating in atmosphere; Age: 3,500; Event: Oldest fossils of cells (prokaryotes); Age: 4,600; Event: Approximate time of origin of Earth

The relative time span shows that from the period of the approximate time of origin of Earth to the present day, around 87% of the time was Pre-Cambrian, 7% was Paleozoic, 3.5% was Mesozoic, and 2.5% Cenozoic.

Earth’s Tectonic Plates

Text description of this image

The details of the map are as follows:

The Pacific Plate extends off the west coast of North and South America (but does not reach the South American coastline; it is separated from the coast by the Nazca plate, described below). A region of violent tectonic activity is highlighted off the southwest side of the Pacific Plate, near the edge of the map in the ocean. The Pacific Plate is moving west and very slightly north.; The Juan de Fuca Plate is a small plate bordering part of the far North American coastline. No direction of movement is indicated for this plate.; The North American Plate encompasses most of North America and extends a little more than halfway across the Atlantic Ocean. A region of violent tectonic activity is highlighted along the west coast of North America, with a few smaller regions noted in the Atlantic Ocean toward the far eastern boundary of the North American Plate. This plate is moving west and slightly north, opposite the Eurasian and African Plates.; The Cocos Plate is a small plate off the west coast of Central America. It is moving northwest, and is surrounded by nearby regions of violent tectonic activity on all but its western boundary.; The Nazca Plate sits of the west coast of most of South America and is directly south of the Cocos Plate and west of the Pacific Plate. No direction of movement is indicated.; The South American Plate encompasses South America and extends out about halfway across the Atlantic Ocean. It is moving west and slightly south. Regions of violent tectonic activity line the west coast of South America with a small dot on the boundary of the South American and Nazca plates.; The Caribbean Plate is a small plate that encompasses southern Central America and extends westward into the ocean above South America. No direction of movement is indicated and a region of violent tectonic activity lines the western region of the plate, alongside the Cocos plate.; The Scotia Plate is just visible in this map off the bottom tip of South America (bordering the South American Plate to the south). No direction of movement is indicated.; The Eurasian plate is a large plate encompassing the Eurasian landmass and extending about halfway across the Atlantic Ocean (where it meets the North American plate). Regions of violent tectonic activity line its eastern edge, its boundary with the Australian Plate (described below) and more sparsely along its boundary with the African and North American plates. Direction of movement is east and slightly south, opposite the North American Plate.; The African Plate sits just south of the Eurasian Plate and encompasses Africa and extends out into the ocean on all sides, meeting the South American, Antarctic, Australian, Indian, Eurasian, and North American Plates. Sparse regions of violent tectonic activity are on the east coast of Africa and in the ocean off the northwest coast of Africa. Direction of movement is east and slightly north, opposite the South American Plate.; The Arabian Plate is a small plate to the northeast of Africa, between the African and Eurasian Plates. Sparse regions of violent tectonic activity are on its southwestern boundary. No direction of movement is indicated.; The Indian Plate is east of the Arabian Plate and south of the Eurasian Plate. No violent tectonic activity is noted. Direction of movement is north and slightly east, into the Eurasian Plate.; The Australian Plate is south of the Indian and Eurasian Plates, encompassing Australia and the surrounding ocean. Regions of violent tectonic activity are dense on its boundaries with the Eurasian and Pacific Plates. Direction of movement is north and slightly west, opposite the Antarctic Plate.; The Antarctic Plate is south of the Australian and African Plates (in this map only ocean is depicted as the map does not show the Antarctic continent). There is a small region of violent tectonic activity in the ocean between the Antarctic and Australian Plates. Direction of movement is south and slightly west, opposite the Australian Plate.; The Philippine Plate borders the Eurasian Plate, the Australian Plate and the Pacific Plate off the east coast of the Eurasian Plate. Regions of violent tectonic activity dot its boundaries and appear in its center. No direction of movement is indicated.

A cutaway view shows the different layers of earth in consecutive circles. At the center is the inner core, next is the outer core, and next is mantle. Outer core and mantle are equally thick. Crust is the outermost layer and is very thin.

The History of Plate Tectonics

Text description of this image

The details of the timeline are as follows:

At the end of the Paleozoic (251 million years ago), all of the Earth’s landmasses were joined in a supercontinent which spanned the equator. Pangaea (the supercontinent) formed about 250 million years ago.; By the mid-Mesozoic era (135 million years ago), Pangaea split into northern (Laurasia) and southern (Godwana) landmasses. These later separated into the modern continents. On the map, Laurasia is shown toward the north of the equator while Godwana is shown toward the south.; By the end of the Mesozoic (65.5 million years ago), Laurasia and Godwana separated into the present-day continents. North America, South America, Eurasia, Africa, Antarctica, India, Madagascar and Australia are all labeled on the map.; During the recent Cenozoic, India collided with Eurasia (just 10 million years ago), forming the Himalayas, the tallest and youngest of Earth’s mountain ranges.

Mechanisms of Macroevolution: Large Effects from Small Genetic Changes

  • Scientists are increasingly able to explain the basic biological mechanisms of macroevolutionary changes seen in the fossil record.
    • Working at the interface of evolutionary biology and developmental biology (evo-devo) scientists are studying how slight changes in the flow of genetic information can become magnified into major structural differences among species.
    • Evolutionary transformations can result from genes that alter the rate, timing, and spatial pattern of changes in an organism’s form as it develops from a zygote into an adult.

Comparison of Human and Chimpanzee Skull Development

Text description of this image

The photo shows that the infant chimpanzee’s face is much flatter than the adult face, which has protruding lower facial features.; The images show a grid is superimposed over all four skulls described.; The grids are square over the fetal skulls but are distorted over the adults, highlighting differences in bone structure in different skull regions.; Similar to the human fetal skull, the chimpanzee fetal skull has a flat face and a wide dome at the back of the skull. The chimpanzee adult has an elongated lower face and very long jawbone, with a much smaller and flatter rounded region at the back of the skull than the other skulls diagrammed. The grid lines are much distorted.; The human adult skull is more similar to the human and chimpanzee fetal skulls than to the chimpanzee adult skull, and retains the shorter jaw of both fetal skulls, the flatter face, and the wide dome at the back of the skull; the grid lines are not very distorted. This is because the human adult skull has paedomorphic features.

A Range of Eye Complexity Among Molluscs

  • Most complex structures have evolved in small steps from simpler versions having the same basic function, a process of refinement rather than the sudden appearance of complexity.
  • The evolution of complex eyes can be traced from a simple ancestral patch of photoreceptor cells through a series of incremental modifications that benefited their owners at each stage.
Text description of this image

Type of eye: Patch of pigmented cells; The figure shows a simple patch of pigmented cells (photoreceptors) on a flat disk is connected to a cable of nerve fibers; Example: Limpet, a mollusc with a round shell; Type of eye: Eyecup; The figure shows an eyecup is a cup-like structure with pigmented cells in the bottom of the “cup” and a cable of nerve fibers extending from the back of the eyecup. A single layer of cells extends to the sides of the eyecup; Example: Abalone, with a rough, domed shell; Type of eye: Simple pinhole eye; The figure shows a spherical structure with a fluid-filled cavity is open at a small point near the front; extensions stretch to the sides of this point. A layer of pigmented cells (the retina) lines the spherical fluid-filled cavity. The optic nerve stretches from the back of the eye; Example: Nautilus, with a crescent-shaped, striped cell; Type of eye: Eye with primitive lens; The figure shows a transparent protective tissue (the cornea) that appears to be a modification of the extensions at the sides of the opening in the pinhole eye now stretches in front of the entire eye. Just beneath the cornea is the lens. The retina lines the spherical fluid-filled cavity beneath the lens and the optic nerve stretches from the back of the eye; Example: Marine snail with a conical shell; Type of eye: Complex camera-lens type eye; The figure shows the cornea is in front of a chamber; at the back of this small chamber is a small lens. Behind the lens is a fluid-filled spherical cavity; the retina lines the back of this cavity. The optic nerve stretches behind the eye; Example: Squid, with many tentacles and a distinct head region

Classifying the Diversity of Life: Classification and Phylogeny

  • Taxonomy is the naming and classification of species.
  • Systematics includes taxonomy and focuses on classifying organisms and determining their evolutionary relationships.
  • Biologists use phylogenetic trees to depict hypotheses about the evolutionary history of species and reflect the hierarchical classification of groups nested within more inclusive groups.
